title: Über die letzten Dinge
summary: "Über die letzten Dinge" by Otto Weininger is a collection of philosophical essays and aphorisms written in the early 20th century. Centered on ethics and metaphysics, it advances a rigorous dualism of cosmos versus chaos, examines crime, madness, genius, time, and culture, and treats art and nature as symbols of moral realities. Readers can expect polemical reflections framed by a biographical preface and daring interpretations (notably of Ibsen’s Peer Gynt) that pursue redemption through truth, responsibility, and inner transformation. The opening of the work presents a biographical preface that sketches the author’s life, studies, and turn from positivism to a Kantian-Platonic ethical dualism, alongside his intense musical sensibility (with Wagner and Beethoven central) and a symbolic reading of nature. It lays out the core thesis: human life is a combat between the “Nothing” (chaos, crime, insanity) and the “All” (goodness, truth), with genius and sainthood defined as the complete overcoming of that inner negation; strict sexual ethics and the earlier book are explained as defenses against moral collapse, culminating in the account of his suicide as a refusal of compromise. Brief letters and notes amplify his symbolist method and moral preoccupations, followed by a table of contents. The first major essay then begins by rejecting fashionable readings of Peer Gynt and recasting it as a universal redemption drama in Kantian terms: love as the path to a true self, the trolls’ self-sufficiency as moral failure, the “button-molder” as the unyielding claim of conscience, and the critique of the lukewarm human who lacks a stable “I,” with Solveig emblematic of salvation.
